title: How do you make an existing List of objects immutable (Collections.unmodifiableList, List.of, deep copy for mutable elements)?
shortTitle: How to make an existing List of objects immutable

s1_definition.profdef: You can make a list unmodifiable in several ways with different guarantees. `Collections.unmodifiableList` wraps an existing list in a read-only view, but changes to the original backing list still show through, so it is only a view. `List.of` and `List.copyOf` create a genuinely independent immutable list that also rejects null elements. However, all of these only make the list structure immutable; the elements themselves are not copied, so if the elements are mutable, callers can still mutate those elements. For true deep immutability you must also deep-copy the elements or store immutable element types.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, making a list immutable is like sealing a folder of documents. `Collections.unmodifiableList` is like putting a clear plastic cover over the bank's own folder so nobody can add or remove pages, but the bank clerk can still slip a page into the original folder underneath, and it shows through. `List.copyOf` is like making a completely separate sealed photocopy folder that nobody, not even the clerk, can change. But even a sealed folder does not stop someone editing the writing on an individual page if the pages themselves can be written on, which is why for a truly tamper-proof record you also need the pages, the elements, to be unchangeable.
s1_definition.oneliner: unmodifiableList is a live read-only view, List.of and List.copyOf are independent immutable lists, but none copy mutable elements — deep-copy elements for true immutability.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You can make a list unmodifiable in several ways with different guarantees. `Collections.unmodifiableList` wraps an existing list in a read-only view, but changes to the original backing list still show through, so it is only a view. `List.of` and `List.copyOf` create a genuinely independent immutable list that also rejects null elements. However, all of these only make the list structure immutable; the elements themselves are not copied, so if the elements are mutable, callers can still mutate those elements. For true deep immutability you must also deep-copy the elements or store immutable element types.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, making a list immutable is like sealing a folder of documents. `Collections.unmodifiableList` is like putting a clear plastic cover over the bank's own folder so nobody can add or remove pages, but the bank clerk can still slip a page into the original folder underneath, and it shows through. `List.copyOf` is like making a completely separate sealed photocopy folder that nobody, not even the clerk, can change. But even a sealed folder does not stop someone editing the writing on an individual page if the pages themselves can be written on, which is why for a truly tamper-proof record you also need the pages, the elements, to be unchangeable.

**One line to remember:** unmodifiableList is a live read-only view, List.of and List.copyOf are independent immutable lists, but none copy mutable elements — deep-copy elements for true immutability.

sections.s2_technical:
`Collections.unmodifiableList(list)` returns a wrapper around the given list. The wrapper throws `UnsupportedOperationException` on any mutating call like add or remove. The important caveat is that it is a view, not a copy. If you keep a reference to the original list and modify it, those modifications are visible through the unmodifiable wrapper, because they share the same backing storage. So it only protects against mutation through the wrapper, not against mutation through the original.

`List.of(a, b, c)`, introduced in Java 9, creates a compact, genuinely immutable list. It copies its arguments into its own internal structure, rejects null elements, and throws on any mutation. `List.copyOf(existing)`, also from Java 9, takes an existing collection and returns an independent immutable copy, so later changes to the source do not affect it. These are the preferred modern tools when you want a true immutable list rather than a mere view.

All of these address structural immutability, meaning you cannot add, remove, or replace elements. None of them copy the elements themselves. So if your list holds mutable objects, a caller who obtains an element reference can still mutate that element. For example, an immutable list of mutable Account objects still lets someone call a setter on an Account.

To achieve deep immutability you have two main options. First, store immutable element types, which is the cleanest, so there is nothing to mutate. Second, when copying the list, also deep-copy each element into an immutable form. A senior nuance is choosing the right tool: use `List.copyOf` when you want a true independent immutable snapshot, use `Collections.unmodifiableList` only when you deliberately want a live read-only view over a list you control, and never expose the backing list. Another nuance is that `Arrays.asList` is fixed-size but still allows set, so it is not immutable, which is a common trap. In banking, the safest default is `List.copyOf` of immutable element types, so both the list and its contents are tamper-proof.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank publishes a list of a customer's recent transactions that must not be altered by any downstream service. This is exactly what an immutable list provides.

Problem 2 — A first attempt used Collections.unmodifiableList but kept mutating the backing list elsewhere, and the changes leaked through the view. This is exactly the view-versus-copy distinction, fixed by List.copyOf.

Problem 3 — The list held mutable transaction objects, and a service mutated an element's note field. This is exactly why deep immutability requires immutable elements, fixed by using an immutable Transaction type.

The code shows an unmodifiable view leaking, a true copy with List.copyOf, and an immutable element type, in an `ImmutableListDemo` main class.
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/history/ImmutableListDemo.java

# Run
java -cp out com.bank.history.ImmutableListDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a backing list starting with one transaction TXN-1, with more transactions added later.

Step 1: The backing list is created with TXN-1. An unmodifiable view is wrapped around it.

Step 2: TXN-2 is added to the backing list. Because the unmodifiable wrapper is only a view over the same backing storage, the view's size becomes 2, showing the change leaked through. This proves unmodifiableList is a view, not a copy.

Step 3: Attempting to add directly through the view throws UnsupportedOperationException, which is caught and logged. The view does block mutation through itself, just not through the original.

Step 4: List.copyOf is called on the backing list, creating an independent immutable snapshot with the current elements. This copy has its own storage.

Step 5: TXN-3 is added to the backing list. The snapshot's size stays the same, because it is a true independent copy. This proves List.copyOf isolates from later backing changes.

Step 6: An element is read from the snapshot. Because Transaction is an immutable type with no setters, there is nothing to mutate on it, so the immutability is deep, not just structural. The record is fully tamper-proof.

```text
WARNING: unmodifiable VIEW leaked backing change, size=2
INFO: view.add blocked
INFO: copyOf SNAPSHOT size stayed = 2
INFO: Element is immutable type, no setter to tamper: TXN-1 SAV2001 Rs.50000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  backing = [TXN-1]
    │ unmodifiableList(backing) → view (SAME backing)
    │ backing.add(TXN-2)
    ▼
  view.size() = 2   ← LEAK (view shares backing)
    │ view.add(...) → UnsupportedOperationException ✓

  List.copyOf(backing) → snapshot [independent copy]
    │ backing.add(TXN-3)
    ▼
  snapshot.size() = 2  ← ISOLATED (no leak)

  elements are immutable Transaction → deep immutability ✓
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Choosing the Right Immutability Tool ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Tool                     view?  independent?   │
  │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────│
  │ Collections.unmodifiableList  YES    NO        │  live read-only view
  │ List.of(a,b,c)                NO     YES        │  no nulls, immutable
  │ List.copyOf(src)              NO     YES        │  snapshot, immutable
  │ Arrays.asList(arr)            --     NO (set OK)│  TRAP: not immutable
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Depth of immutability:
   STRUCTURAL : cannot add/remove/replace  (all tools above)
   DEEP       : elements also unchangeable  (needs immutable elements
                OR deep-copied elements)

  Banking default:
   List.copyOf( list of immutable Transaction ) → structural + deep
   Never expose the backing list reference.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
There are several ways to make a list immutable, and the key is knowing exactly what each one guarantees. Collections dot unmodifiableList wraps an existing list in a read-only view that throws on any mutation through the wrapper. The critical caveat is that it is a view, not a copy, so if I keep a reference to the original backing list and modify it, those changes leak through the wrapper because they share the same storage. It only protects against mutation through the wrapper itself.

List dot of and List dot copyOf, from Java 9 onward, are different. They create a genuinely independent immutable list. List dot of builds one from explicit elements, and List dot copyOf takes an existing collection and returns an independent immutable snapshot, so later changes to the source do not affect it. They also reject null elements. These are my preferred tools when I want a true immutable list rather than a live view.

The subtle point that trips people up is that all of these only provide structural immutability, meaning you cannot add, remove, or replace elements. None of them copy the elements themselves. So an immutable list of mutable objects still lets a caller obtain an element and mutate it through a setter. To get deep immutability I either store immutable element types, which is cleanest, or deep-copy each element when building the list.

So my practical guidance is this. Use List dot copyOf when I want a true independent immutable snapshot, which is almost always what I want. Use Collections dot unmodifiableList only when I deliberately want a live read-only view over a list I fully control, and never expose the backing list. And I watch out for the common trap that Arrays dot asList is fixed-size but still allows set, so it is not immutable at all. In our banking history service, the safe default is List dot copyOf of immutable Transaction objects, which gives both structural and deep immutability, so I can hand the same snapshot to analytics, fraud checks, and statement generation at once, with zero risk that any of them corrupts the customer's transaction history.
